body:
A complete story of the problems I faced and the solutions that finally worked

When I first tried to build a real time notification system using the MERN stack, I thought it would be a simple feature. All I needed was a small alert that appeared instantly whenever something changed on the server. But, like many things in full-stack development, it quickly turned into a series of unexpected challenges.

This article walks through my exact journey: the problems I encountered, the wrong turns, and the techniques that finally helped me build a ready real time system with WebSockets and Node.js.

The Problem: Why Real Time Notifications Felt Harder Than Expected

The idea was simple. I wanted users to see updates instantly without refreshing the page. It could be new messages, order updates, comments, or system alerts.

My first attempt was the classic “beginner mistake”: using setInterval to repeatedly fetch new data from the backend. It worked for a few minutes. Then it started breaking. CPU usage climbed. API calls multiplied. The server slowed down.

I realised I was not building a notification system.
I was building a problem.

I needed proper real-time communication. That meant WebSockets.

Issue #1: The WebSocket Connection Kept Disconnecting

The first issue happened immediately. My client connected, then disconnected every 20 30 seconds. At first, I blamed my code, but the actual problem was how WebSockets work behind the scenes.

The root causes were:

  1. My server did not properly handle ping/pong heartbeats.
  2. I was trying to host the backend behind a reverse proxy without WebSocket upgrade headers.

Once I fixed the server configuration and added heartbeat support, the stability instantly improved.

Issue #2: Notifications Were Delivered, But the UI Did Not Update

This one was very confusing. The backend was sending real-time notifications. I could see them arrive in the browser console. But the React UI ignored them completely.

The problem was the React state was not updating because the component listening for events was unmounted and remounted on route changes.

The professional solution was to build a global event listener using React Context.

Once I implemented a dedicated NotificationContext, the UI updated instantly anywhere in the app.

Issue #3: Multiple Users Received the Wrong Notifications

In the first version, every connected client received all notifications. That meant User A saw alerts meant for User B.

This was happening because I wasn’t mapping user IDs to socket connections. Professional real-time systems always track socket sessions.

I solved this by:

  1. Storing each connected user’s socket ID in a Map.
  2. Updating the Map on connect and disconnect.
  3. Sending notifications only to the socket belonging to the user the message was intended for.

This is exactly how platforms like Facebook or Slack deliver user-specific real-time events.

How I Finally Built a Professional Real Time Notification System

Backend Setup (Node.js + Express + Socket.io)

The backend handles connection, stores user sockets, and sends targeted notifications.

const express = require('express');
const http = require('http');
const { Server } = require('socket.io');

const app = express();
const server = http.createServer(app);

const io = new Server(server, {
    cors: {
        origin: '*'
    }
});

const onlineUsers = new Map();

io.on('connection', socket => {
    socket.on('register', userId => {
        onlineUsers.set(userId, socket.id);
    });

    socket.on('disconnect', () => {
        for (const [userId, socketId] of onlineUsers.entries()) {
            if (socketId === socket.id) {
                onlineUsers.delete(userId);
            }
        }
    });
});

// Send notification to a specific user
function sendNotification(userId, message) {
    const socketId = onlineUsers.get(userId);
    if (socketId) {
        io.to(socketId).emit('notification', message);
    }
}

server.listen(5000);

Frontend Setup (React + Socket.io-client)

React receives notifications through a global context.

import { createContext, useEffect, useState } from 'react';
import { io } from 'socket.io-client';

export const NotificationContext = createContext();

export const NotificationProvider = ({ children, userId }) => {
    const [notifications, setNotifications] = useState([]);
    const socket = io('http://localhost:5000');

    useEffect(() => {
        socket.emit('register', userId);

        socket.on('notification', data => {
            setNotifications(prev => [...prev, data]);
        });

        return () => {
            socket.disconnect();
        }
    }, []);

    return (
        <NotificationContext.Provider value={{ notifications }}>
            {children}
        </NotificationContext.Provider>
    );
};

Displaying Notifications in the UI

import { useContext } from 'react';
import { NotificationContext } from './NotificationContext';

function NotificationBell() {
    const { notifications } = useContext(NotificationContext);

    return (
        <div>
            Notifications: {notifications.length}
        </div>
    );
}

How I Ensured It Was Ready

1. Implemented Heartbeats

This prevents broken connections from staying alive.

2. Used a Reverse Proxy That Supports WebSockets

Nginx configuration had to include:

proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";

3. Stored Notifications in MongoDB

So users don’t lose notifications when offline.

4. Added Authentication

Each WebSocket connection is authenticated using a token.

5. Introduced Message Acknowledgments

To prevent losing notifications when the network is unstable.

Final Result

Notifications now appear instantly across the app without refreshing.
Each user receives only their alerts.
The system remains stable even under hundreds of simultaneous users.

This solution is now part of my standard MERN architecture whenever I need real-time features.

conclusion

Building real time systems is more complex than it looks. You must understand connection stability, error handling, state management, and user-specific routing. The issues I faced taught me that real-time communication is not just a technical feature; it requires the same planning and professionalism as any other major system in your application.
